newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac takes huge risk with early vote.
newsitem.headline: Chirac takes huge risk with early vote.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac has taken a gamble that may make or break his presidency by calling a snap parliamentary election he says is needed to revitalise France for the introduction of a single European currency.
Opposition parties blasted the early poll as a ploy to pave the way for a new bout of fiscal austerity while hiding the failings of the centre-right government behind a rushed campaign.

Socialist leader Lionel Jospin said Chirac was veering towards a harsher Anglo-Saxon brand of capitalism. Far right National Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen accused Chirac of an "electoral hold-up, a shameful swindle".

Once nicknamed the "bulldozer" for his blunt style, Chirac said he was bringing forward the National Assembly vote by more than nine months to let voters "express themselves clearly on the scale and speed of change over the next five years".
The election will be held in two rounds on May 25 and June 1.
Victory will ensure 64-year-old Chirac a renewed, if reduced, majority in parliament for the remaining five years of his presidency.

But defeat could reduce him to a lame duck overshadowed by a prime minister Jospin. It is only the fifth time a president has called an early election since the start of the Fifth Republic in 1958 -- and the first when no serious crisis is looming.
"It's a serious game of poker," said Iain Lindsay, senior bond analyst at Credit Lyonnais. "The outcome is far from a foregone conclusion."
Conservative Prime Minister Alain Juppe, who came to power with Chirac in 1995, will present his coalition's election platform in a keynote policy speech on Tuesday (1330 GMT).
The main worry for French voters is unemployment -- which has risen to 12.8 percent of the workforce from 11.7 percent when Chirac took office two years ago promising a war for jobs.
Chirac said he was calling the early vote partly to ensure France was ready for decisions on closer European integration in 1998, which he said would bring extra prosperity and security.

"To approach these deadlines from a position of strength, to build a Europe that respects the genius of its member nations and is capable of rivalling the great world blocs, your agreement and support are essential," Chirac said.

The European Union will decide early in 1998 which nations qualify for a single currency. Jospin says Chirac's EU arguments are empty because the Socialists also favour the single currency -- but not at the price of an extra bout of austerity.
Chirac also justified the vote by saying that "together we must deeply reform the state to allow a cut in public spending, the only way to cut taxes and charges that weigh too heavily on you."
Jospin said the government also wanted to go to the polls before corruption scandals engulfed some of its leading members.

The government has denied opposition charges that the budget deficit is set to overshoot three percent of Gross Domestic Product for 1997, a criterion for qualifying for European economic and monetary union (EMU), perhaps reaching even 3.8 percent.

Opinion polls show that the centre-right, which now has 464 members out of 577 seats in the National Assembly, could lose about 150 seats in a snap vote but still retain a majority. The coalition also has about a dozen allies in parliament

The prospect of weeks of political uncertainty with an outside chance of a left-wing win unsettled financial markets. The CAC-40 bourse index ended the day down 0.98 percent after losing 2.59 percent last Friday as election speculation mounted.
